claim: Divisive normalization of neural responses by the activity of neighboring neurons has been proposed as a fundamental operation in the nervous system based on its success in predicting neural responses recorded in primate electrophysiology studies.
source: Divisive normalization of the neural responses by the activity of the neighboring neurons has been proposed as a fundamental operation in the nervous system based on its success in predicting neural responses recorded in primate electrophysiology studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior research in primate electrophysiology.

claim: Experimental evidence for the existence of normalization in the human brain is still scant.
source: Nevertheless, experimental evidence for the existence of this operation in the human brain is still scant.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature and existing evidence.

claim: The response to multiple stimuli can generally be better described by a model that takes normalization into account compared to weighted sum and weighted average models.
source: we first modeled single-voxel responses using a weighted sum, a weighted average, and a normalization model and demonstrated that although the weighted sum and weighted average models also made acceptable predictions in some conditions, the response to multiple stimuli could generally be better described by a model that takes normalization into account.
evidence: This claim is based on the modeling results comparing three different models against fMRI data.

claim: The effects of attention on cortical responses are predicted by the normalization model but not by the weighted sum or weighted average models.
source: We then determined the observed effects of attention on cortical responses and demonstrated that these effects were predicted by the normalization model, but not by the weighted sum or the weighted average models.
evidence: This claim is based on comparing model predictions with observed attentional effects in the data.

claim: Evidence of normalization operation in higher regions of the monkey visual cortex has been demonstrated both during passive viewing and when attention is directed towards a stimulus.
source: evidence of its operation in higher regions of the monkey visual cortex has also been demonstrated both during passive viewing (Bao and Tsao, 2018) and when attention is directed towards a stimulus (Reynolds and Heeger, 2009; Lee and Maunsell, 2010; Ni et al., 2012; Ni and Maunsell, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to monkey electrophysiology studies.

claim: Normalization has been proposed as a critical operation in the human brain based on evidence demonstrating the sublinear addition of responses to multiple stimuli in the visual cortex.
source: Normalization has also been proposed as a critical operation in the human brain based on evidence demonstrating the sublinear addition of responses to multiple stimuli in the visual cortex (Bloem and Ling, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bloem and Ling, 2019.

claim: A weighted average model can account for multiple-stimulus responses in the monkey brain.
source: Nevertheless, in lieu of directly testing the normalization model to resolve multiple-stimulus representation, several previous studies have shown that a weighted average model can account for multiple-stimulus responses in the monkey brain (Zoccolan et al., 2005; Macevoy and Epstein, 2009; Reddy et al., 2009; Kliger and Yovel, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: In the category-selective regions of the monkey brain, a winner-take-all, but not averaging, rule can explain neural responses in many cases.
source: The only exception is a recent electrophysiology study, which showed that in the category-selective regions of the monkey brain, a winner-take-all, but not averaging, rule can explain neural responses in many cases (Bao and Tsao, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bao and Tsao, 2018.

claim: The normalization model predicts winner-take-all behavior.
source: Bao and Tsao, 2018 further demonstrated that the normalization model predicts such winner-take-all behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bao and Tsao, 2018.

claim: Attention works through increasing the response gain or contrast gain of the attended stimulus.
source: Attention works through increasing the response gain (Treue and Martínez Trujillo, 1999; McAdams and Maunsell, 1999) or contrast gain (Reynolds et al., 2000; Martínez-Trujillo and Treue, 2002) of the attended stimulus.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on attention mechanisms.

claim: Normalization attenuates the neural response in proportion to the activity of the neighboring neuronal pool.
source: They have suggested that normalization attenuates the neural response in proportion to the activity of the neighboring neuronal pool (Reynolds and Heeger, 2009; Ni et al., 2012; Boynton, 2009; Lee et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on normalization and attention.

claim: Different forms of attention (space-based and feature-based) have distinctions in their reported effects, such as different time courses and the extent to which they affect different locations in the visual field.
source: While it has been suggested that these different forms of attention affect neural responses in similar ways, there exist distinctions in their reported effects, such as different time courses (Hayden and Gallant, 2005) and the extent to which they affect different locations in the visual field (Serences and Boynton, 2007; Womelsdorf et al., 2006), suggesting that there are common sources as well as differences in modulation mechanisms between these forms of attention (Ni and Maunsell, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies comparing different forms of attention.

claim: Normalization has been speculated to underlie response modulations in the presence of attention in the human visual cortex, with evidence provided by behavioral and neuroimaging studies.
source: In the human visual cortex, normalization has been speculated to underlie response modulations in the presence of attention, with evidence provided both by behavioral studies of space-based (Herrmann et al., 2010) and feature-based (Herrmann et al., 2012; Schwedhelm et al., 2016) attention, as well as neuroimaging studies of feature-based attention (Bloem and Ling, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to behavioral and neuroimaging studies.

claim: Evidence for directly testing the validity of the normalization model in predicting human cortical responses in a quantitative way remains scarce.
source: Although previous studies have qualitatively suggested the role of normalization in the human visual cortex (Bloem and Ling, 2019; Kliger and Yovel, 2020; Itthipuripat et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016), evidence for directly testing the validity of the normalization model in predicting human cortical responses in a quantitative way remains scarce.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature.

claim: A few studies have demonstrated the quantitative advantage of normalization-based models compared to linear models in predicting human fMRI responses using gratings, noise patterns, single objects, and moving checkerboards.
source: A few studies have demonstrated the quantitative advantage of normalization-based models compared to linear models in predicting human fMRI responses using gratings, noise patterns, and single objects (Kay et al., 2013a; Kay et al., 2013b), as well as moving checkerboards (Aqil et al., 2021; Foster and Ling, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating normalization advantages.

claim: Normalization is closer to average in the absence of attention.
source: We also demonstrate that normalization is closer to average in the absence of attention, as previously reported by several studies (Zoccolan et al., 2005; Macevoy and Epstein, 2009; Kliger and Yovel, 2020), but that the results of the weighted average model and the normalization model diverge to a greater extent in the presence of attention.
evidence: This claim is based on the study's findings and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The results of the weighted average model and the normalization model diverge to a greater extent in the presence of attention.
source: We also demonstrate that normalization is closer to average in the absence of attention, as previously reported by several studies (Zoccolan et al., 2005; Macevoy and Epstein, 2009; Kliger and Yovel, 2020), but that the results of the weighted average model and the normalization model diverge to a greater extent in the presence of attention.
evidence: This claim is based on the study's findings.

claim: Participants viewed semi-transparent gray-scale stimuli from the two categories of houses and human bodies.
source: In a blocked-design fMRI paradigm, human participants (N = 19) viewed semi-transparent gray-scale stimuli from the two categories of houses and human bodies (Figure 1a).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The experiment had a total number of eight conditions (four isolated, three paired, and one fixation conditions).
source: The experiment, therefore, had a total number of eight conditions (four isolated, three paired, and one fixation conditions, see Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the experimental design and is illustrated in Figure 1c.

claim: The two stimuli were superimposed in paired blocks to minimize the effect of spatial attention and force participants to use object-based attention.
source: In paired blocks, we superimposed the two stimuli to minimize the effect of spatial attention and force participants to use object-based attention (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: This describes the experimental design rationale and is shown in Figures 1b and 1c.

claim: The overall average accuracy was higher than 86% in all conditions.
source: Overall, the average accuracy was higher than 86% in all conditions.
evidence: This is a direct report of behavioral performance data.

claim: Post-hoc t-tests showed that the significant effect of condition on accuracy and reaction time was due to lower performance in the BatH and BHat conditions.
source: As expected, post-hoc t-tests showed that this was due to lower performance in the BatH and BHat conditions (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The observation that attended stimuli elicit higher responses than unattended stimuli is in agreement with previous research indicating that attention to objects increases their cortical responses.
source: This is in agreement with previous research indicating that attention to objects increases their cortical responses (Reddy et al., 2009; Roelfsema et al., 1998; O'Craven et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on attention effects.

claim: In the body-selective region EBA, the response to attended body stimuli in isolation is similar to the response to attended body stimuli paired with unattended house stimuli.
source: For instance, in the body-selective region EBA, the response to attended body stimuli in isolation is similar to the response to attended body stimuli paired with unattended house stimuli (compare Bat and BatH bars).
evidence: This is an observation from the fMRI data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In EBA, the response to attended house stimuli in the isolated condition is significantly less than the response to attended house stimuli paired with unattended body stimuli.
source: On the other hand, the response to attended house stimuli in the isolated condition is significantly less than the response to attended house stimuli paired with unattended body stimuli.
evidence: This is an observation from the fMRI data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the object-selective regions LO and pFs, almost half of the voxels were selective to each category.
source: As illustrated in the figure, in the object-selective regions LO and pFs, almost half of the voxels were selective to each category
evidence: This is based on voxel preference analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claim: In the EBA and PPA regions, the general preference of the region prevailed.
source: while in the EBA and PPA regions, the general preference of the region prevailed
evidence: This is based on voxel preference analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The mean voxel response was generally higher when each stimulus was attended compared to the condition in which it was ignored.
source: We observed that the mean voxel response was generally higher when each stimulus was attended compared to the condition in which it was ignored.
evidence: This is based on analysis of fMRI responses across conditions.

claim: The effect of attention was absent or only marginally significant in V1.
source: In all cases, the effect of attention was absent or only marginally significant in V1
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of fMRI data.

claim: Attentional effects are much weaker or even absent in V1 compared to the higher-level regions of the occipito-temporal cortex.
source: which is not surprising since attentional effects are much weaker (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999) or even absent (Luck et al., 1997) in V1 compared to the higher-level regions of the occipito-temporal cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on attention in V1.

claim: The normalization model was a better fit for the data compared to the weighted sum (ps < 0.02) and the weighted average (ps < 0.0001) models.
source: As observed in the figure, the normalization model was a better fit for the data compared to the weighted sum (ps < 0.02) and the weighted average (ps < 0.0001) models.
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model fits shown in Figure 3f.

claim: The normalization model was a better fit according to the AIC measure as well.
source: Since the normalization model had more parameters, we also used the AIC measure to correct for the difference in the number of parameters. The normalization model was a better fit according to the AIC measure as well (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on AIC analysis to account for model complexity.

claim: The normalization model was equally successful across ROIs in predicting the explainable variation in the data.
source: demonstrating that the normalization model was equally successful across ROIs in predicting the explainable variation in the data.
evidence: This is inferred from the NRD analysis showing no significant differences across ROIs.

claim: For the paired condition in which none of the stimuli were attended (the PN condition), the results of the weighted average model were closer to normalization.
source: Interestingly, just focusing on the paired condition in which none of the stimuli were attended (the PN condition), the results of the weighted average model were closer to normalization
evidence: This is an observation from the model comparison results.

claim: The weighted average model provides good predictions of neural and voxel responses in the absence of attention.
source: These results are in agreement with previous studies suggesting that the weighted average model provides good predictions of neural and voxel responses in the absence of attention (Zoccolan et al., 2005; Macevoy and Epstein, 2009; Kliger and Yovel, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and the current data.

claim: When considering all the attended and unattended conditions, the normalization model is a generally better fit across all ROIs.
source: However, when considering all the attended and unattended conditions, our results show that the normalization model is a generally better fit across all ROIs.
evidence: This is based on the overall model comparison results.

claim: Simulation results demonstrate that despite the higher number of parameters, the normalization model is only a better fit for the population of normalizing neurons and not for summing or averaging neurons.
source: Our simulation results demonstrate that despite the higher number of parameters, the normalization model is only a better fit for the population of normalizing neurons and not for summing or averaging neurons, as illustrated in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The better fits of the normalization model cannot be related to the model's nonlinearity or its higher number of parameters.
source: These results confirm that the better fits of the normalization model cannot be related to the model's nonlinearity or its higher number of parameters.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: Shifting attention from the preferred to the null stimulus caused a reduction in voxel responses.
source: First, for the paired conditions, shifting attention from the preferred to the null stimulus caused a reduction in voxel responses.
evidence: This is based on analysis of fMRI responses across attention conditions.

claim: The effect of the unattended stimulus on the response depended on voxel selectivity for that stimulus, with the unattended preferred stimulus having larger effects on the response than the unattended null stimulus.
source: The second feature we observed was that the effect of the unattended stimulus on the response depended on voxel selectivity for that stimulus, with the unattended preferred stimulus having larger effects on the response than the unattended null stimulus.
evidence: This is based on analysis of fMRI responses showing asymmetry in attentional modulation.

claim: Attending to the preferred stimulus in the presence of the null stimulus caused the response to approach the response elicited when attending to the isolated preferred stimulus.
source: Attending to the preferred stimulus in the presence of the null stimulus caused the response to approach the response elicited when attending to the isolated preferred stimulus.
evidence: This is an observation from the fMRI data.

claim: Attention effectively removed the effect of the null stimulus.
source: Therefore, attention effectively removed the effect of the null stimulus.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that attending to the preferred stimulus yields responses similar to isolated preferred stimulus responses.

claim: Attending to the null stimulus in the presence of the preferred stimulus did not eliminate the effect of the preferred stimulus and yielded a response well above the response elicited by attending to the isolated null stimulus.
source: However, attending to the null stimulus in the presence of the preferred stimulus did not eliminate the effect of the preferred stimulus and yielded a response well above the response elicited by attending to the isolated null stimulus.
evidence: This is an observation from the fMRI data.

claim: This is the first time such asymmetry has been reported in human fMRI studies.
source: While this is the first time such asymmetry has been reported in human fMRI studies, these results are in agreement with previous monkey electrophysiology studies, showing the existence of an asymmetry in attentional modulation for attention to the preferred versus the null stimulus (Lee and Maunsell, 2010; Ni et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding in human fMRI.

claim: The asymmetry in attentional modulation is in agreement with previous monkey electrophysiology studies.
source: While this is the first time such asymmetry has been reported in human fMRI studies, these results are in agreement with previous monkey electrophysiology studies, showing the existence of an asymmetry in attentional modulation for attention to the preferred versus the null stimulus (Lee and Maunsell, 2010; Ni et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to monkey electrophysiology studies.

claim: When attention shifted from the preferred to the null stimulus, there was a significant reduction in response in multiple regions of interest in the occipito-temporal cortex but not in the primary visual area.
source: we showed that when attention shifted from the preferred to the null stimulus, there was a significant reduction in response in multiple regions of interest in the occipito-temporal cortex but not in the primary visual area.
evidence: This is based on analysis of fMRI responses across attention conditions.

claim: The response reduction with attention shift increased as we moved to higher regions across the hierarchy.
source: Furthermore, this response reduction increased as we moved to higher regions across the hierarchy, consistent with speculations of greater effects of top-down attention on higher regions of the visual cortex (Cook and Maunsell, 2002).
evidence: This is based on analysis of fMRI responses and supported by citation.

claim: The predictions of the weighted average model were significantly lower than the response reduction observed in the data in all ROIs except in V1.
source: our results showed that the predictions of the weighted average model were significantly lower than the response reduction observed in the data in all ROIs except in V1.
evidence: This is based on comparing model predictions with observed data.

claim: The normalization model predicted the response reduction more accurately in all regions except in V1, where no significant response reduction was observed.
source: In contrast, the normalization model predicted the response reduction more accurately in all regions except in V1, where no significant response reduction was observed.
evidence: This is based on comparing model predictions with observed data.

claim: Attention to a preferred stimulus almost eliminates the effect of the ignored null stimulus.
source: We demonstrated that while attention to a preferred stimulus almost eliminates the effect of the ignored null stimulus, attention to the null stimulus does not remove the effect of the preferred stimulus.
evidence: This is based on analysis of fMRI responses showing asymmetry in attentional modulation.

claim: Attention to the null stimulus does not remove the effect of the preferred stimulus.
source: We demonstrated that while attention to a preferred stimulus almost eliminates the effect of the ignored null stimulus, attention to the null stimulus does not remove the effect of the preferred stimulus.
evidence: This is based on analysis of fMRI responses showing asymmetry in attentional modulation.

claim: The asymmetry measured by the defined index remains approximately the same in all regions.
source: Unlike response change with the shift of attention, which increases across the hierarchy, the asymmetry measured by our defined index remains approximately the same in all regions
evidence: This is based on analysis of the asymmetry index across ROIs.

claim: The asymmetry depends not on the top-down attentional signal but on the normalization computation performed in each region.
source: indicating its dependence not on the top-down attentional signal but on the normalization computation performed in each region.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that asymmetry is constant across regions.

claim: The asymmetry feature was predicted by the normalization model but not by the weighted sum and the weighted average models.
source: This feature was also predicted by the normalization model but not by the weighted sum and the weighted average models.
evidence: This is based on comparing model predictions with observed asymmetry.

claim: Normalization has been reported to cause neural populations to operate in the averaging or winner-take-all regimes based on stimulus contrast.
source: Normalization has been reported to cause neural populations to operate in the averaging or winner-take-all regimes based on stimulus contrast (Busse et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Busse et al., 2009.

claim: In the presence of attention, responses can deviate from the averaging regime even without a change in contrast.
source: Here, we showed that in the presence of attention, responses can deviate from the averaging regime even without a change in contrast.
evidence: This is based on the study's findings about attention effects.

claim: A winner-take-all behavior was observed when the preferred stimulus was attended since its higher response along with its increase in gain due to attention made it a much stronger input compared to the ignored null stimulus.
source: We observed a winner-take-all behavior when the preferred stimulus was attended since its higher response along with its increase in gain due to attention, made it a much stronger input compared to the ignored null stimulus.
evidence: This is based on analysis of fMRI responses in different attention conditions.

claim: When the null stimulus was attended, the response was closer to an average than a max-pooling response.
source: On the other hand, when the null stimulus was attended, the response was closer to an average than a max-pooling response.
evidence: This is based on analysis of fMRI responses in different attention conditions.

claim: A combination of bottom-up and top-down signals act to yield a response that can be the average of the isolated responses, or a winner-take-all response, or somewhere between the two.
source: We, therefore, extend previous reports of multiple-stimulus representation showing that the response is related to stimulus contrast (Busse et al., 2009) and neural selectivity (Bao and Tsao, 2018) by demonstrating that a combination of bottom-up and top-down signals act to yield a response that can be the average of the isolated responses, or a winner-take-all response, or somewhere between the two.
evidence: This is based on the study's findings and extends previous work.

claim: The normalization model is superior to the weighted average model in its ability to account for fMRI responses in the presence of attention.
source: We also demonstrate for the first time that the normalization model is superior to the weighted average model, which has often been used in lieu of the normalization model (Zoccolan et al., 2005; Macevoy and Epstein, 2009; Kliger and Yovel, 2020), in its ability to account for fMRI responses in the presence of attention.
evidence: This is based on the study's model comparison results.

claim: Responses to strong high-contrast stimuli are added sublinearly to yield the multiple-stimulus response, as predicted by the normalization model and the weighted average model.
source: While responses to strong high-contrast stimuli are added sublinearly to yield the multiple-stimulus response, as predicted by the normalization model and the weighted average model, the sublinearity decreases for lower contrasts and even changes to linearity and supralinearity for weak stimuli (Heuer and Britten, 2002; Rubin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on contrast effects.

claim: The sublinearity decreases for lower contrasts and even changes to linearity and supralinearity for weak stimuli.
source: While responses to strong high-contrast stimuli are added sublinearly to yield the multiple-stimulus response, as predicted by the normalization model and the weighted average model, the sublinearity decreases for lower contrasts and even changes to linearity and supralinearity for weak stimuli (Heuer and Britten, 2002; Rubin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The weighted average model generally performs better than the weighted sum model in the higher-level occipito-temporal cortex.
source: Our results demonstrate that while the weighted average model generally performs better than the weighted sum model in the higher-level occipito-temporal cortex, the weighted sum model provides better predictions in V1.
evidence: This is based on the study's model comparison results.

claim: The weighted sum model provides better predictions in V1.
source: Our results demonstrate that while the weighted average model generally performs better than the weighted sum model in the higher-level occipito-temporal cortex, the weighted sum model provides better predictions in V1.
evidence: This is based on the study's model comparison results.

claim: The results suggest stronger sublinearity in higher regions of the visual cortex compared to V1.
source: These results suggest stronger sublinearity in higher regions of the visual cortex compared to V1, which is in agreement with previous reports (Kay et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is inferred from the model comparison results and supported by citation.

claim: V1 neurons have higher sensitivity to contrast.
source: This observation might be related to the higher sensitivity of V1 neurons to contrast (Goodyear and Menon, 1998)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Goodyear and Menon, 1998.

claim: Higher sensitivity to contrast causes a more significant decrease in V1 responses to low-contrast stimuli.
source: causing a more significant decrease in V1 responses to low-contrast stimuli.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher sensitivity of V1 to contrast.

claim: A more significant decrease in V1 responses to low-contrast stimuli might make the low-contrast stimulus weaker for V1 neurons, causing a move toward a lower level of sublinearity.
source: This, in turn, might make the low-contrast stimulus weaker for V1 neurons, causing a move toward a lower level of sublinearity (Sceniak et al., 1999).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning supported by citation to Sceniak et al., 1999.

claim: Attention to a stimulus has been suggested to be similar to an increase in the contrast of the attended stimulus.
source: Attention to a stimulus has been suggested in the literature to be similar to an increase in the contrast of the attended stimulus (Ni et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ni et al., 2012.

claim: The similar effects of attention and contrast are manifested in the normalization equation.
source: which is manifested in the similar effects of attention and contrast in the normalization equation.
evidence: This is based on the mathematical formulation of the normalization model.

claim: To fully ascertain the role of normalization in the human brain, we have to measure the contrast response function in each voxel to truly constrain the models and have conditions with varying levels of contrasts across attentional manipulations.
source: We acknowledge that to fully ascertain the role of normalization in the human brain, we have to measure the contrast response function in each voxel to truly constrain the models and have conditions with varying levels of contrasts across attentional manipulations.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study.

claim: The results remain suggestive of the role of normalization until conditions with varying contrasts are tested in future multi-session experiments.
source: Our results remain suggestive of the role of normalization until these conditions are tested in future multi-session experiments.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations and future directions.

claim: Cross-validation and the AIC measure were used to ensure that the difference in the number of free parameters did not affect the results.
source: To ensure that the difference in the number of free parameters did not affect the results, we used cross-validation and the AIC measure to compare model predictions with the data.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach to account for model complexity.

claim: If the success of the normalization model was due to its higher number of free parameters, it would affect its predictions for left-out data.
source: If the success of the normalization model was due to its higher number of free parameters, it would affect its predictions for left-out data.
evidence: This is a logical statement about model validation.

claim: The normalization model was successful in predicting the left-out part of the data.
source: We observed that the normalization model was also successful in predicting the left-out part of the data.
evidence: This is based on cross-validation results.

claim: A nonlinear model variant with five free parameters was still a worse fit than the normalization model.
source: In addition, we tested a nonlinear model variant with five free parameters. This model was still a worse fit than the normalization model.
evidence: This is based on model comparison results.

claim: Simulation results confirmed that the success of the normalization model is not due to its nonlinearity or the higher number of parameters but rather as a result of it being a closer estimation of the computation performed at the neural level for object representation.
source: Simulation results demonstrated that the normalization model was a better fit only for the normalizing population, confirming that the success of the normalization model is not due to its nonlinearity or the higher number of parameters but rather as a result of it being a closer estimation of the computation performed at the neural level for object representation.
evidence: This is based on simulation results.

claim: The BOLD response is an indirect measure of the activity of neural populations.
source: We are aware of the limitations of the fMRI technique as the BOLD response is an indirect measure of the activity of neural populations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about fMRI.

claim: An increase in the BOLD signal could be related to an increase in the neuronal firing rates of the local population.
source: While an increase in the BOLD signal could be related to an increase in the neuronal firing rates of the local population (Logothetis et al., 2001)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Logothetis et al., 2001.

claim: An increase in the BOLD signal could also be related to subthreshold activity resulting from feedback from the downstream regions of the visual cortex.
source: it could also be related to subthreshold activity resulting from feedback from the downstream regions of the visual cortex (Heeger and Ress, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Heeger and Ress, 2002.

claim: The observed effects may be related to local population responses or may be influenced by feedback from downstream regions.
source: The observed effects, therefore, may be related to local population responses or may be influenced by feedback from downstream regions.
evidence: This is inferred from the nature of BOLD signals.

claim: Since the measured BOLD signal is related to the average activity of the local population, some effects may change in the averaging process.
source: Also, since the measured BOLD signal is related to the average activity of the local population, and we do not have access to single-unit responses, some effects may change in the averaging process.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of fMRI.

claim: Simulation results show that the effects of the normalization computation are preserved even after averaging.
source: Nevertheless, our simulation results show that the effects of the normalization computation are preserved even after averaging.
evidence: This is based on simulation results.

claim: The simulations are not based on data directly measured from neurons.
source: We should keep in mind, though, that these are only simulations and are not based on data directly measured from neurons.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the simulations.

claim: Future experiments with intracranial recordings from neurons in the human visual cortex would be invaluable in validating the results.
source: Future experiments with intracranial recordings from neurons in the human visual cortex would be invaluable in validating our results.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: A possible stronger saturation of the BOLD response can potentially explain the observed asymmetry in attentional modulation.
source: Another limitation in interpreting the results is related to a possible stronger saturation of the BOLD response, which can potentially explain the observed asymmetry in attentional modulation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about alternative explanations.

claim: The asymmetry in attentional modulation has been previously reported at the neural level.
source: Since the asymmetry in attentional modulation has also been previously reported at the neural level (Ni et al., 2012), this effect is unlikely to be exclusively caused by the saturation in the BOLD signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ni et al., 2012.

claim: Saturation is a characteristic of cortical responses even at the neural level.
source: It is noteworthy, however, that saturation is a characteristic of cortical responses even at the neural level.
evidence: This is established knowledge about neural responses.

claim: Whether the asymmetry effect at the neural level is caused by response saturation or as a result of the normalization computation cannot be distinguished from current knowledge.
source: Whether this effect at the neural level is caused by response saturation or as a result of the normalization computation cannot be distinguished from our current knowledge.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current understanding.

claim: A variant of the weighted average model with an extra saturation parameter could partially predict the observed asymmetry, but the predictions were worse than the normalization model's predictions.
source: Nevertheless, we tested a variant of the weighted average model with an extra saturation parameter. Although this model could partially predict the observed asymmetry, the predictions were worse than the normalization model's predictions.
evidence: This is based on model comparison results.

claim: The saturation model was an overall worse fit to the data compared to the normalization model.
source: Also, this model was an overall worse fit to the data compared to the normalization model.
evidence: This is based on model comparison results.

claim: The normalization model provides a more parsimonious account of the data.
source: The normalization model, therefore, provides a more parsimonious account of the data.
evidence: This is inferred from the model comparison results.

claim: The exact nonlinearities that affect the transformation of neural population responses to the BOLD response are not fully mapped out yet, especially in cases where multiple overlapping stimuli are presented in the visual scene.
source: The exact nonlinearities that affect the transformation of neural population responses to the BOLD response are not fully mapped out yet, especially in cases where multiple overlapping stimuli are presented in the visual scene.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current knowledge.

claim: It is possible that the advantage of the normalization model could be at least partly related to nonlinearities in the transformation from neural responses to BOLD.
source: It is possible that the advantage of the normalization model could be at least partly related to these nonlinearities.
